name: Iowa
uniformActsAdopted: Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006), enacted 2014, with Sections 109, 119 and 120 varied
Uniform Probate Code — Iowa Probate Code, chapter 633 (adult guardianship and conservatorship rewritten 2019, in force 1 January 2020)
Iowa Trust Code, chapter 633A, with a non-uniform certification of trust at §633A.4604
Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (2015), enacted 2017 (short title drops “Revised”)
Revised Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (2006), chapter 142C
note: Iowa is the jurisdiction in this set that most often makes a legal effect turn on **what the relying party knows, or on a clock**, rather than on the instrument. A health-care agent outranks a court-appointed guardian only while “known to the health care provider to be available and willing” (§144B.6(1)); the holder of the right to control a body forfeits it on a murder charge only once “those charges are known to a third party”, and forfeits it outright by not acting within 24 hours of notification or 40 hours of death (§144C.8); an agent’s authority ends when the agent is “named as having abused the principal in a **founded dependent adult abuse report**” — a confidential administrative finding (§633B.110(2)(e)) — while the same registry is what the court must search before appointing a guardian (§633.564). Elsewhere Iowa is the uniform power of attorney act with a mandatory notary and Alternative A, a conservatorship that **suspends and then reinstates** the agency rather than ending or continuing it (§633B.108(2)), a surrogate who can only co-sign with the physician (§144A.7), the only certification of trust with a remedy for refusing it (§633A.4604(6)), and a $50,000 small-estate route that prices refusal and acceptance alike and obliges the custodian to answer whether the estate qualifies (§633.356).

citations.title: Title
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the “Iowa Uniform Power of Attorney Act”. 2014 Acts, ch 1078, §3

citations.title: Durability of power of attorney
citations.quote: A power of attorney created under this chapter is durable unless the power of attorney expressly provides that it is terminated by the incapacity of the principal.

citations.title: Execution
citations.quote: A power of attorney must be signed by the principal or in the principal’s conscious presence by another individual, other than any prospective agent, directed by the principal to sign the principal’s name on the power of attorney. A power of attorney must be acknowledged before a notary public or other individual authorized by law to take acknowledgments. An agent named in the power of attorney shall not notarize the principal’s signature. An acknowledged signature on a power of attorney is presumed to be genuine.

citations.title: Nomination of conservator or guardian — relation of agent to court-appointed fiduciary
citations.quote: 1. Under a power of attorney, a principal may nominate a conservator of the principal’s estate or guardian of the principal’s person for consideration by the court … Except for good cause shown or disqualification, the court shall make its appointment in accordance with the principal’s most recent nomination. … 2. If, after a principal executes a power of attorney, a court appoints a conservator of the principal’s estate or other fiduciary charged with the management of some or all of the principal’s property, the power of attorney is suspended unless the power of attorney provides otherwise or unless the court appointing the conservator decides the power of attorney should continue. If the power of attorney continues, the agent is accountable to the fiduciary as well as to the principal. The power of attorney shall be reinstated upon termination of the conservatorship as a result of the principal regaining capacity.

citations.title: When power of attorney effective
citations.quote: 1. A power of attorney is effective when executed unless the principal provides in the power of attorney that it becomes effective at a future date or upon the occurrence of a future event or contingency. 2. If a power of attorney becomes effective upon the occurrence of a future event or contingency, the principal, in the power of attorney, may authorize one or more persons to determine in a writing or other record that the event or contingency has occurred. 3. If a power of attorney becomes effective upon the principal’s incapacity and the principal has not authorized a person to determine whether the principal is incapacitated or the person authorized is unable or unwilling to make the determination, the power of attorney becomes effective upon a determination in a writing or other record by the occurrence of any of the following: a. A licensed physician or licensed psychologist determines that the principal is incapacitated. b. A judge, or an appropriate governmental official determines that the principal is incapacitated. 4. A person authorized by the principal in the power of attorney to determine that the principal is incapacitated may act as the principal’s personal representative pursuant to the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 … to obtain access to the principal’s health care information and to communicate with the principal’s health care provider.

citations.title: Termination — power of attorney or agent authority
citations.quote: 2. An agent’s authority terminates when any of the following occurs: a. The principal revokes the authority. b. The agent dies, becomes incapacitated, or resigns. c. An action is filed for the dissolution or annulment of the agent’s marriage to the principal or for their legal separation, unless the power of attorney otherwise provides. d. The power of attorney terminates. e. The agent is named as having abused the principal in a founded dependent adult abuse report. f. The agent is convicted of dependent adult abuse for having abused the principal. … 4. Termination of a power of attorney or an agent’s authority under this section is not effective as to the agent or another person that, without actual knowledge of the termination, acts in good faith under the power of attorney.

citations.title: Acknowledged power of attorney — acceptance and reliance
citations.quote: 4. A person that is asked to accept an acknowledged power of attorney may request, and rely upon, all of the following without further investigation: a. An agent’s certification under penalty of perjury of any factual matter concerning the principal, agent, or power of attorney in substantially the same form as set out in section 633B.302. b. An English translation … c. An opinion of agent’s counsel … 5. An English translation or an opinion of counsel requested under this section shall be provided at the principal’s expense unless the request is made more than ten business days after the power of attorney is presented for acceptance.

citations.title: Refusal to accept acknowledged power of attorney — liability
citations.quote: 1. … a. A person shall either accept an acknowledged power of attorney or request a certification, a translation, or an opinion of counsel … no later than seven business days after presentation … b. If a person requests a certification … the person shall accept the power of attorney no later than five business days after receipt … c. A person shall not require an additional or different form of power of attorney for authority granted in the power of attorney presented unless an exception in subsection 2 applies. 2. A person is not required to accept an acknowledged power of attorney if any of the following occurs: … e. The person in good faith believes that the power of attorney is not valid or that the agent does not have the authority to perform the act requested, or that the power of attorney does not comply with federal or state law or regulations, whether or not a certification, a translation, or an opinion of counsel … has been requested or provided. f. The person makes, or has actual knowledge that another person has made, a report to the department of health and human services stating a good-faith belief that the principal may be subject to physical or financial abuse, neglect, exploitation, or abandonment by the agent … 3. A person that refuses to accept an acknowledged power of attorney in violation of this section is subject to both of the following: a. A court order mandating acceptance … b. Liability for damages sustained by the principal and reasonable attorney fees and costs … provided that any such action must be brought within one year of the initial request for acceptance of the power of attorney.

citations.title: Definitions
citations.quote: 3. “Durable power of attorney for health care” means a document authorizing an attorney in fact to make health care decisions for the principal if the principal is unable, in the judgment of the attending physician or attending physician assistant, to make health care decisions.

citations.title: Durable power of attorney for health care
Requirements
citations.quote: 1. … b. The durable power of attorney for health care contains the date of its execution and is witnessed or acknowledged by one of the following methods: (1) Is signed by at least two individuals who, in the presence of each other and the principal, witnessed the signing … (2) Is acknowledged before a notarial officer within this state as provided in chapter 9B. … 3. At least one of the witnesses … shall be an individual who is not a relative of the principal by blood, marriage, or adoption within the third degree of consanguinity.

citations.title: Individuals ineligible to be attorney in fact
Attorney in fact — priority to make decisions
citations.quote: 1. Unless the district court sitting in equity specifically finds that the attorney in fact is acting in a manner contrary to the wishes of the principal or the durable power of attorney for health care provides otherwise, an attorney in fact who is known to the health care provider to be available and willing to make health care decisions has priority over any other person, including a guardian appointed pursuant to chapter 633, to act for the principal in all matters of health care decisions. The attorney in fact has authority to make a particular health care decision only if the principal is unable, in the judgment of the attending physician or attending physician assistant, to make the health care decision. If the principal objects to a decision to withhold or withdraw health care, the principal shall be presumed to be able to make a decision.

citations.title: Procedure in absence of declaration
citations.quote: 1. Life-sustaining procedures may be withheld or withdrawn from a patient who is in a terminal condition and who is comatose, incompetent, or otherwise physically or mentally incapable of communication and has not made a declaration in accordance with this chapter if there is consultation and written agreement for the withholding or the withdrawal of life-sustaining procedures between the attending physician and any of the following individuals, who shall be guided by the express or implied intentions of the patient, in the following order of priority if no individual in a prior class is reasonably available, willing, and competent to act: a. The attorney in fact designated to make treatment decisions … if the designation is in writing and complies with chapter 144B. b. The guardian of the person of the patient if one has been appointed, provided court approval is obtained … c. The patient’s spouse. d. An adult child of the patient or, if the patient has more than one adult child, a majority of the adult children who are reasonably available for consultation. e. A parent of the patient, or parents if both are reasonably available. f. An adult sibling. 2. When a decision is made pursuant to this section to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining procedures, there shall be a witness present at the time of the consultation when that decision is made.

citations.title: Letters
citations.quote: Upon the filing of an oath of office or certification and a bond, if any is required, the clerk shall issue letters under the seal of the court, giving the fiduciary the powers authorized by law.

citations.title: Order of preference for appointment of executor
Distribution of property by affidavit — very small estates
citations.quote: 1. When the gross value of the decedent’s personal property that would otherwise be distributed by will or intestate succession is or has been, at any time since the decedent’s death, fifty thousand dollars or less and there is no real property … and if forty days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, a successor as defined in subsection 2 may, by furnishing an affidavit … and without procuring letters of appointment … … 4. … b. If the evidence of ownership is not presented to the holder of the property, the holder may require, as a condition for the payment, delivery, or transfer of the property, that the affiant provide the holder with a bond in a reasonable amount determined by the holder to be sufficient to indemnify the holder … … 6. … b. If the holder of the decedent’s property refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer any property … within a reasonable time, a successor may recover the property or compel its payment … the court shall award attorney fees to the person bringing the action if the court finds that the holder … acted unreasonably in refusing … 7. b. … If an action is brought against the holder under this section, the court shall award attorney fees to the holder if the court finds that the holder acted reasonably in paying, delivering, or transferring the property as required by this section. … 9. Upon receipt of an affidavit under subsection 3 and reasonable proof under subsection 5 of the identity of each successor … the holder of the property shall disclose to the affiant whether the value of the property held by the holder is, or has been at any time since the decedent’s death, fifty thousand dollars or less. … 2025 amendments to section apply retroactively to January 1, 2025, to the estates of decedents dying on or after January 1, 2025; 2025 Acts, ch 148, §54

citations.title: Basis for appointment of guardian for an adult
Basis for appointment of conservator for an adult
Petition for appointment of guardian or conservator for an adult
Background check of proposed guardian or conservator
citations.quote: 1. The court shall request criminal record checks and checks of the child abuse, dependent adult abuse, and sexual offender registries in this state for all proposed guardians and conservators, other than financial institutions with Iowa trust powers, unless a proposed guardian or conservator has undergone the background check required by this section within the twelve months prior to the filing of a petition … 2. The court shall review the results of background checks in determining the suitability of a proposed guardian or conservator for appointment. … 4. The person who files a petition … shall be responsible for paying the fee for the background check …

citations.title: Qualifications and selection of guardian or conservator for an adult
citations.quote: The court shall appoint as guardian or conservator for an adult any qualified and suitable person who is willing to serve as guardian or conservator.

citations.title: Appointment of guardian for an adult on a standby basis
Emergency appointment of temporary guardian or conservator
Notification of guardianship and conservatorship powers
Certification of trust
citations.quote: 1. A trustee may present a certification of trust to any person in lieu of providing a copy of the trust instrument … 2. The certification of trust must do all of the following: a. State the names of all the currently acting trustees. b. If there is more than one currently acting trustee, state whether the trustees may act individually or must act by majority decision or must act by unanimous decision. c. State that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended … d. Be signed by a currently acting trustee or the attorney of an acting trustee. e. Be dated and certified under penalty of perjury … or be subscribed and sworn to under penalty of perjury before a notary public … 4. A person may require that the trustee offering the certification of trust provide proof of the trustee’s identity and copies of those excerpts from the original trust instrument … 5. A person who acts in reliance upon a certification of trust after taking reasonable steps to verify the identity of the trustee and without knowledge that the representations contained in the certification are incorrect is not liable … The period of time to verify the identity of the trustee shall not exceed ten business days from the date the person received the certification of trust. … 6. A person making a demand for the trust instrument in addition to a certification of trust or excerpts shall be liable for damages, including attorney fees, incurred as a result of the refusal to accept the certification of trust.

citations.title: Short title
citations.quote: This chapter may be cited as the “Iowa Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act”. 2017 Acts, ch 79, §4

citations.title: User direction for disclosure of digital assets
citations.quote: 1. A user may use an online tool to direct the custodian to disclose to the designated recipient or not to disclose some or all of the user’s digital assets, including the content of electronic communications. If the online tool allows the user to modify or delete a direction at any time, a direction regarding disclosure using an online tool overrides a contrary direction by the user in a will, trust, power of attorney, or other record.

citations.title: Custodian compliance and immunity
citations.quote: 1. Not later than sixty days after receipt of the information required under sections 638.7 through 638.15, a custodian shall comply with a request under this chapter from a fiduciary or designated recipient to disclose digital assets or terminate an account. If the custodian fails to comply, the fiduciary or designated recipient may apply to the court for an order directing compliance.

citations.title: Persons who may make — manner of making — amending or revoking — refusal to make anatomical gift before donor’s death — preclusive effect
citations.quote: 1. Who may make. … an anatomical gift of a donor’s body or part may be made during the life of the donor … by any of the following: a. The donor if the donor is any of the following: (1) An adult. … (3) A minor, if the minor is authorized under state law to apply for a driver’s license or identification card because the minor is at least fourteen years of age … with the signed approval of a parent or guardian. (4) A minor, if the minor is authorized under state law to apply for a hunting, fishing, or fur harvester license … b. An agent of the donor, unless the durable power of attorney for health care or other record prohibits the agent from making the anatomical gift. c. A parent of the donor, if the donor is an unemancipated minor. d. The guardian of the donor.

citations.title: Who may make anatomical gift of decedent’s body or part — amending or revoking gift
Effect of anatomical gift on advance health care directive
Final disposition of remains — right to control
citations.quote: 1. … the right to control final disposition of a decedent’s remains … vests in and devolves upon the following persons who are competent adults at the time of the decedent’s death, in the following order: a. A designee, or alternate designee, acting pursuant to the decedent’s declaration. b. The surviving spouse … c. A surviving child … or, if there is more than one, a majority of the surviving children … … i. A person who represents that the person knows the identity of the decedent and who signs an affidavit warranting the identity of the decedent and assuming the right to control final disposition of the decedent’s remains and the responsibility to pay any expense attendant to such final disposition …

citations.title: Forfeiture of authority to control
citations.quote: A designee or person with the authority to control under this chapter shall forfeit all rights and authority under a declaration, or by operation of section 144C.5 … under either of the following circumstances: 1. The designee or person with the authority to control under this chapter is charged with murder in the first or second degree or voluntary manslaughter in connection with the declarant’s death and those charges are known to a third party. 2. The designee or person with the authority to control under this chapter does not exercise the designee’s authority under the declaration within twenty-four hours of receiving notification of the death of the declarant or within forty hours of the declarant’s death, whichever is earlier. 2008 Acts, ch 1051, §13, 22; 2025 Acts, ch 22, §3

citations.title: Relation of agent to court-appointed fiduciary
citations.quote: [The power of attorney is not terminated and the agent’s authority continues unless limited, suspended, or terminated by the court.] … Comment … Section 108(b) is a departure from the Uniform Durable Power of Attorney Act which gave a court-appointed fiduciary the same power to revoke or amend a power of attorney as the principal would have if not incapacitated.

patches.diff:
Iowa took the Uniform Power of Attorney Act in 2014 (§633B.101, “Iowa Uniform Power of Attorney Act”, 2014 Acts ch. 1078) and §633B.104 is the uniform §104 default: durable unless the instrument “expressly provides that it is terminated by the incapacity of the principal”.

Three Iowa variations matter, and all three are about the relying party rather than the principal.

**§633B.105 makes notarisation a condition of validity**, as West Virginia does — a power “must be acknowledged before a notary public” — and adds a conflict rule the uniform act lacks: “An agent named in the power of attorney shall not notarize the principal’s signature.” Iowa then still takes **Alternative A** at §633B.120, owing the duty to accept on *any* acknowledged power. That combination is the counterexample to the pattern the four Alternative states suggested: a harder instrument to create does not go with a narrower duty to accept.

**§633B.120(1)(c) prohibits a ground of refusal outright** — “A person shall not require an additional or different form of power of attorney for authority granted in the power of attorney presented”. Nebraska enumerates two unlawful grounds in a list of its own; Iowa writes one into the duty itself, so insisting on the bank’s own form is a breach rather than an unlisted excuse.

**§633B.120(2)(e) then gives most of it back.** A person need not accept where it “in good faith believes that the power of attorney is not valid or that the agent does not have the authority to perform the act requested … **whether or not** a certification, a translation, or an opinion of counsel … has been requested or provided”. The evidence the act tells a relying party it may demand is expressly made incapable of curing its doubt.

And §633B.120(3)(b) puts a **one-year limitation period** on the remedy, running from “the initial request for acceptance” — the only clock on a fee shift in this reference.

Possible but against the grain, since §633B.104 reverses the common-law default: an Iowa power is nondurable only where it says so expressly. §633B.110(1)(b) then terminates it on the principal’s incapacity, and §633B.110(5) protects an agent or third party who acts in good faith “without actual knowledge of the incapacity” — so the terminating event is again one the relying party may not know has happened.

§633B.109 is the uniform §109, and Iowa’s additions solve a problem no other jurisdiction in this reference addresses.

The principal may name “one or more persons to determine **in a writing or other record** that the event or contingency has occurred” (§633B.109(2)). If nobody was named, or the named person will not act, a power springing on incapacity becomes effective on a written determination by “a licensed physician or licensed psychologist” or by “a judge, or an appropriate governmental official” (§633B.109(3)).

Then §633B.109(4): the person authorised to determine incapacity “may act as the principal’s personal representative pursuant to the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 … to obtain access to the principal’s health care information and to communicate with the principal’s health care provider”.

That closes a loop every other springing-power regime leaves open. Determining incapacity requires medical information; obtaining medical information requires authority; and the authority is what the determination is supposed to switch on. Iowa grants the determiner federal health-records standing for the sole purpose of making the determination.

localNames: durable power of attorney for health care
patches.diff:
A separate and much older act: chapter 144B, the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care (1991 Acts ch. 140), not the 2014 financial act.

**Its formalities run the opposite way from the financial power.** §144B.3(1)(b) accepts **either** two witnesses who sign in each other’s and the principal’s presence **or** acknowledgment before a notarial officer, where §633B.105 requires the notary outright; and §144B.3(3) requires at least one witness who is not a relative “within the third degree of consanguinity”. So in Iowa the document that refuses treatment is easier to execute than the one that moves money — the inverse of Missouri, where §404.810 makes the health-care power the most formal instrument in this data.

Authority starts on a clinical judgement: the agent may act only where the principal is unable “in the judgment of the attending physician or attending physician assistant” (§§144B.1(3), 144B.6(1)), and if the principal objects to a withholding decision they “shall be presumed to be able to make a decision”.

§144B.6(1) then settles the contest with a later court appointment in the agent’s favour — the agent “has priority over any other person, **including a guardian** appointed pursuant to chapter 633” — but conditions that priority on something outside the instrument: it holds for an agent “**who is known to the health care provider to be available and willing** to make health care decisions”. The agent’s rank depends on the relying party’s state of knowledge.

patches.summary: Iowa's default surrogate is not a substitute decision maker: §144A.7 requires written agreement between the ranked relative and the attending physician, witnessed, and only to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining procedures in a terminal condition.
patches.diff:
Iowa has one, but it is not the role this baseline describes, and the difference is the point: **the Iowa surrogate cannot decide. It can only agree.**

§144A.7(1) permits life-sustaining procedures to be withheld or withdrawn from a patient who left no declaration only where there is “consultation and **written agreement** for the withholding or the withdrawal … **between the attending physician and**” one of a ranked list: the §144B attorney in fact; the guardian, but only with court approval under §633.635(3)(b)(1); the spouse; an adult child, or “a majority of the adult children who are reasonably available”; a parent or both parents; an adult sibling. §144A.7(2) additionally requires **a witness present at the consultation**.

Everywhere else in this data a surrogate is a substitute decision maker whose standing the relying party has to assess. In Iowa the decision is a jointly signed instrument, so there is nothing for the surrogate to prove and no moment at which they hold authority alone. The authority is the agreement, not the person.

Two limits are worth recording. The power reaches **only** withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining procedures from a patient in a terminal condition who is comatose or incapable of communication — it is not a general health-care surrogacy, so an Iowa patient with no instrument has no one who can consent to ordinary treatment by operation of law. And §144A.7(3) suspends the whole section for a patient known to the attending physician to be pregnant with a fetus that could develop to live birth.

Iowa rewrote adult guardianship in 2019 (2019 Acts ch. 57, in force 1 January 2020), repealing the former §633.570 outright. §633.552 sets the basis for appointment, §633.556 the petition, §633.635 the guardian’s responsibilities, and §633.568 and §633.569 the standby and emergency routes.

Two provisions bear on the artefact.

**§633.564 makes vetting mandatory**: the court “shall request criminal record checks and checks of the **child abuse, dependent adult abuse, and sexual offender registries**” for every proposed guardian and conservator — except a financial institution with Iowa trust powers — unless an equivalent check was done in the preceding twelve months, and the petitioner pays for it. Kansas conditions its letters on the appointee having been *trained*; Iowa conditions the appointment on the appointee having been *screened*. Both are fitness gates that precede the document, and neither appears on it.

**§633.178 does not carry the scope.** Letters issue on an oath and any required bond, “giving the fiduciary the powers authorized by law” — a generic grant, where Kansas requires every limitation to be stated on the letters themselves. §633.570 gives the *respondent* written notice of the powers the court may grant, so the person whose rights are at stake is told the scope and the party later asked to honour it is not.

Against the health-care lane the guardian loses: §144B.6(1) ranks a known, willing §144B agent ahead of a guardian, and §144A.7(1)(b) lets a guardian join a life-sustaining-procedures agreement only with court approval.

Appointed under §633.553 for an adult, with powers at §633.642, the same §633.564 background check and the same generic letters under §633.178.

What the appointment does to an existing power of attorney is **a sixth answer** to a question four other states in this set answer four different ways. §633B.108(2): the power of attorney “is **suspended** unless the power of attorney provides otherwise or unless the court appointing the conservator decides the power of attorney should continue” — and then “**The power of attorney shall be reinstated upon termination of the conservatorship as a result of the principal regaining capacity.**”

So Iowa neither terminates the agency (West Virginia, Kentucky) nor continues it (Virginia) nor allocates between the two (Missouri) nor hands the conservator the principal’s revocation power (Nebraska, Kansas). It makes the instrument **dormant and self-reviving**. The paper in the agent’s hand is valid throughout, ineffective in the middle, and effective again at the end, and nothing is reissued or endorsed at either boundary.

§633B.108(1) also binds the court to the principal’s nomination “except for good cause shown or disqualification”.
Chapter 633, the Iowa Probate Code. §633.294 sets the order of preference for appointment, §633.299 the order appointing, and §633.178 issues letters on an oath and any bond required.

The same chapter 633 machinery and the same §633.178 letters. §633.356(10) confines the affidavit route to cases where “no administration of the decedent’s estate is pending”, so the two are alternatives rather than stages.

§633.356 reaches **$50,000** of personal property after **40 days**, “without procuring letters of appointment” — and it is the most fully worked out provision of its kind in this reference, because it legislates the transaction from both sides.

**It prices refusal and acceptance alike.** §633.356(6)(b): where the holder refuses to pay or transfer “within a reasonable time”, the successor may compel it and “the court **shall** award attorney fees to the person bringing the action if the court finds that the holder … acted **unreasonably** in refusing”. §633.356(7)(b): in the same action “the court **shall** award attorney fees **to the holder** if the court finds that the holder acted **reasonably**”. Every other acceptance regime here funds only the claimant; Iowa funds whichever side was reasonable, which makes reasonableness the whole question rather than the validity of the affidavit.

**It lets the claimant ask.** §633.356(9): on receiving the affidavit and identity proof, “the holder of the property **shall disclose to the affiant** whether the value of the property held by the holder is, or has been at any time since the decedent’s death, fifty thousand dollars or less”, and an affidavit furnished for that purpose need not assert the value at all. The one fact that decides whether the route is available is held by the custodian, and Iowa obliges it to answer. Nothing else in this data gives the claimant a query.

**It prices the risk in collateral.** §633.356(4)(b): where evidence of ownership is not produced, the holder may require “a bond in a reasonable amount **determined by the holder**” to indemnify it, or an agreement in lieu. Missouri’s bonds are set by the court; Iowa’s by the counterparty.

**And the state is a rival claimant on a clock.** §633.356(2)(c) makes the Iowa Medicaid agency a statutory “successor”, and §633.356(8)(b) lets the department present its own affidavit where no family affidavit has arrived **within ninety days** of death — submitting “proof of payment of funeral expenses as verification of the decedent’s death **instead of** a certified death certificate”. Nebraska concedes that the death certificate may lag by naming a substitute artefact; Iowa names a different substitute and gives it to the state.

Two further details: §633.356(5) requires “reasonable proof of the identity of each successor … to the satisfaction of the holder”, and §633.356(1) now admits **no real property at all** — the earlier allowance for realty passing to inheritance-tax-exempt joint tenants survives only for deaths before 1 January 2025.

The Iowa Trust Code (§633A.1101), and §633A.4604 is a certification of trust that is not the Uniform Trust Code’s §1013 — Iowa’s is the only one in this reference with **a duty, a remedy and a clock**.

**§633A.4604(6) is the finding, once stated correctly:** “A person making a demand for the trust instrument in addition to a certification of trust or excerpts shall be **liable for damages, including attorney fees**, incurred as a result of the refusal to accept the certification of trust.” This note used to say that everywhere else a counterparty insisting on the whole instrument is merely being difficult, and that was wrong — Uniform Trust Code §1013(h) already makes such a person liable for damages, and Kansas (§58a-1013(h)), Indiana (§30-4-4-5(h)), Colorado (§15-5-1013(8)) and Arizona (§14-11013(H)) all carry it. **What Iowa actually did is delete the condition**: everywhere else liability arrives only “if the court determines that the person did not act in good faith”, which is the hardest thing a claimant can be asked to prove; Iowa's attaches to the demand itself and includes attorney fees as of right. Conditional everywhere, unconditional here — the same axis §120's Alternatives A and B run on.

**§633A.4604(5) puts a clock on diligence:** reliance is protected where the person took “reasonable steps to verify the identity of the trustee”, and “the period of time to verify the identity of the trustee shall not exceed **ten business days**” — the trust-lane counterpart of §633B.120’s seven business days, which no other Uniform Trust Code state here has.

**And §633A.4604(4) makes identity explicit**, letting the person require “proof of the trustee’s identity” along with the excerpts that designate the trustee. The content list is otherwise narrower than the uniform one — no taxpayer identification number, no settlor identity — but it requires **all** currently acting trustees to be named with whether they act individually, by majority or unanimously, and it may be signed by “a currently acting trustee **or the attorney of an acting trustee**”, which is the only place in this data where counsel can sign the artefact instead of the fiduciary.

Consistent with the baseline. §638.4(1) is the uniform online-tool rule and §638.4(3) overrides a contrary terms-of-service provision that the user did not have to accept “affirmatively and distinctly”. The act is at §§638.1 to 638.18 (2017 Acts ch. 79) and its short title — “Iowa Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act” — **drops the “Revised”**, as West Virginia’s and Missouri’s do.

The uniform route, with §638.15 carrying the duties of care, loyalty and confidentiality across to digital assets, barring use of the authority “to impersonate the user”, and making the fiduciary an authorised user for the purposes of Iowa’s computer-fraud section §716.6B. §638.16 gives the custodian sixty days and immunises good-faith compliance; §638.14 deals with disclosure to a conservator or guardian.

Revised Uniform Anatomical Gift Act, §§142C.1 et seq. §142C.3(1) lists who may make a gift during the donor’s life — including “an agent of the donor, unless the durable power of attorney for health care or other record prohibits” it — and Iowa extends the donor class to a **minor of at least fourteen** who authorises the symbol on a driver’s licence **or on a hunting, fishing or fur harvester licence**, with a parent’s signed approval. §142C.4 ranks the post-mortem classes and §142C.12B resolves a conflict between a gift and an advance directive by requiring the physician and donor, or the donor’s agent, to confer.

Disposition of remains is a separate chapter, 144C, and it carries **the sharpest termination rule in this reference**. §144C.5 ranks the right to control, from a designee under a declaration down through the family to a last class found nowhere else: “a person who represents that the person knows the identity of the decedent and who **signs an affidavit warranting the identity** of the decedent and assuming the right to control … and the responsibility to pay any expenses”.

Then §144C.8 takes the authority away on two triggers, each of which makes the loss turn on something other than the holder.

- The holder is “**charged** with murder in the first or second degree or voluntary manslaughter in connection with the declarant’s death **and those charges are known to a third party**”. Virginia ends an agent’s authority on *conviction*; Iowa ends this one on a *charge*, and makes the effect conditional on a third party knowing about it.
- The holder “does not exercise the designee’s authority under the declaration **within twenty-four hours of receiving notification of the death** of the declarant **or within forty hours of the declarant’s death, whichever is earlier**”.

The second is the only authority in this entire data set that lapses for **non-exercise**. Every other role ends on death, revocation, incapacity, a court order or a conviction — all events about the principal or the holder. Iowa ends this one because nobody acted in time, and the clock can expire before the holder is even told.
